source: When gliding by the Bashee isles we emerged at last upon the great South Sea; were it not for other things, I could have greeted my dear Pacific with uncounted thanks, for now the long supplication of my youth was answered; that serene ocean rolled eastwards from me a thousand leagues of blue.

There is, one knows not what sweet mystery about this sea, whose gently awful stirrings seem to speak of some hidden soul beneath; like those fabled undulations of the Ephesian sod over the buried Evangelist St. John. And meet it is, that over these sea-pastures, wide-rolling watery prairies and Potters’ Fields of all four continents, the waves should rise and fall, and ebb and flow unceasingly; for here, millions of mixed shades and shadows, drowned dreams, somnambulisms, reveries; all that we call lives and souls, lie dreaming, dreaming, still; tossing like slumberers in their beds; the ever-rolling waves but made so by their restlessness.

To any meditative Magian rover, this serene Pacific, once beheld, must ever after be the sea of his adoption. It rolls the midmost waters of the world, the Indian ocean and Atlantic being but its arms. The same waves wash the moles of the new-built Californian towns, but yesterday planted by the recentest race of men, and lave the faded but still gorgeous skirts of Asiatic lands, older than Abraham; while all between float milky-ways of coral isles, and low-lying, endless, unknown Archipelagoes, and impenetrable Japans. Thus this mysterious, divine Pacific zones the world’s whole bulk about; makes all coasts one bay to it; seems the tide-beating heart of earth. Lifted by those eternal swells, you needs must own the seductive god, bowing your head to Pan.

But few thoughts of Pan stirred Ahab’s brain, as standing like an iron statue at his accustomed place beside the mizen rigging, with one nostril he unthinkingly snuffed the sugary musk from the Bashee isles (in whose sweet woods mild lovers must be walking), and with the other consciously inhaled the salt breath of the new found sea; that sea in which the hated White Whale must even then be swimming. Launched at length upon these almost final waters, and gliding towards the Japanese cruising-ground, the old man’s purpose intensified itself. His firm lips met like the lips of a vice; the Delta of his forehead’s veins swelled like overladen brooks; in his very sleep, his ringing cry ran through the vaulted hull, “Stern all! the White Whale spouts thick blood!”

modern_en.title: Chapter 111 — The Pacific
paragraphs: As we glided past the Bashee isles, we emerged at last upon the great South Sea. Were it not for other things, I could have greeted my dear Pacific with uncounted thanks, for now the long prayer of my youth was answered: that serene ocean rolled eastward from me a thousand leagues of blue.

There is some sweet mystery about this sea — no one knows quite what — whose gently awesome stirrings seem to speak of some hidden soul beneath — like those fabled heavings of the Ephesian sod over the buried Evangelist St. John. And it is fitting that over these sea-pastures, wide-rolling watery prairies and Potters' Fields of all four continents, the waves should rise and fall, and ebb and flow unceasingly; for here millions of mixed shades and shadows, drowned dreams, sleepwalkings, reveries — all that we call lives and souls — lie dreaming, dreaming, still; tossing like sleepers in their beds; the ever-rolling waves made so only by their restlessness.

To any meditative Magian rover, this serene Pacific, once seen, must forever after be the sea of his adoption. It rolls the midmost waters of the world, the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic being only its arms. The same waves wash the breakwaters of the newly built Californian towns, planted only yesterday by the most recent race of men, and bathe the faded but still gorgeous skirts of Asiatic lands older than Abraham; while between them all float milky ways of coral islands, and low-lying, endless, unknown archipelagoes, and impenetrable Japans. Thus this mysterious, divine Pacific girdles the world's whole bulk; makes all coasts one bay to it; seems the tide-beating heart of the earth. Lifted by those eternal swells, you cannot help but acknowledge the seductive god, bowing your head to Pan.

But few thoughts of Pan stirred Ahab's brain as, standing like an iron statue at his accustomed place beside the mizzen rigging, with one nostril he unthinkingly sniffed the sugary musk from the Bashee isles (in whose sweet woods mild lovers must be walking), and with the other consciously breathed in the salt breath of the newfound sea — that sea in which the hated White Whale must even then be swimming. Launched at last upon these almost final waters, and gliding toward the Japanese cruising ground, the old man's purpose intensified. His firm lips met like the lips of a vise; the Delta of his forehead's veins swelled like overloaded brooks; even in his sleep, his ringing cry ran through the vaulted hull: "Stern all! The White Whale spouts thick blood!"

modern_da.title: Kapitel 111 — Stillehavet
paragraphs: Da vi gled forbi Bashee-øerne, kom vi endelig ud på det store Sydhav. Hvis ikke det havde været for andre ting, kunne jeg have hilst mit kære Stillehav med utallige tak, for nu var min ungdoms lange bøn blevet hørt: Det fredfyldte hav rullede østpå fra mig i tusind mil af blåt.

Der er noget sødt mystisk over dette hav — ingen ved helt hvad — hvis blidt ærefrygtindgydende bevægelser synes at tale om en skjult sjæl dybt nede, som den sagnomspundne hæven sig i jorden over den begravede evangelist Sankt Johannes i Efesos. Og det er passende, at bølgerne over disse havenges vidtrullende vandprærier og alle fire kontinenters Potters' Fields, de fattiges kirkegårde, uophørligt stiger og falder, strømmer og ebber; for her ligger millioner af blandede skygger og skikkelser, druknede drømme, søvngængerier og dagdrømme — alt, hvad vi kalder liv og sjæle — og drømmer, drømmer stadig; de vender sig som sovende i deres senge, og de evigt rullende bølger er kun bølger på grund af deres uro.

For enhver grublende, magiker-agtig vandrer må dette rolige Stillehav, når han først har set det, for altid blive det hav, han har valgt som sit eget. Det ruller verdens midterste vande, og det Indiske Ocean og Atlanterhavet er kun dets arme. De samme bølger skyller mod havnemolerne i de nybyggede californiske byer, grundlagt i går af den nyeste menneskerace, og de bader de falmede, men stadig prægtige skørter på asiatiske lande, der er ældre end Abraham; og imellem dem alle flyder mælkeveje af koraløer og lavtliggende, endeløse, ukendte øgrupper og ugennemtrængelige Japaner. Således omgiver dette mystiske, guddommelige Stillehav hele jordens masse, gør alle kyster til én bugt for sig og synes at være jordens tidevandsbankende hjerte. Løftet af disse evige dønninger kan man ikke andet end anerkende den forførende gud og bøje hovedet for Pan.

Men kun få tanker om Pan rørte sig i Ahabs hjerne, da han stod som en jernstatue på sin sædvanlige plads ved mesanvantet og med det ene næsebor uden at tænke over det snusede den sukkersøde moskusduft fra Bashee-øerne (i hvis søde skove milde elskende må gå og vandre) og med det andet bevidst indåndede den salte ånde fra det nyfundne hav — det hav, hvori den forhadte hvide hval netop da måtte svømme. Nu da han endelig var sat ud på disse næsten sidste farvande og gled mod det japanske fangstfelt, blev den gamle mands forsæt kun stærkere. Hans faste læber lukkede sig som skruestikkens kæber; deltaet af årer i hans pande svulmede som overfyldte bække; selv i søvne gjaldede hans ringende råb gennem det hvælvede skrog: »Bak! Den hvide hval sprøjter tykt blod!«
